discovery: Discovery that living cells organise matter through liquid-liquid phase separation into biomolecular condensates, and the physical theory of active condensates

nominees.name: Clifford P. Brangwynne
nominees.affiliation: Princeton University / Howard Hughes Medical Institute, USA

nominees.name: Anthony A. Hyman
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Dresden, Germany

nominees.name: Frank Jülicher
nominees.affiliation: Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems, Dresden, Germany

subfield: Biological physics / soft condensed matter and statistical physics
motivation: In 2009 Brangwynne, Hyman and Jülicher showed that P granules in C. elegans embryos are liquid droplets that condense and dissolve by phase separation, controlled by concentration gradients. This revealed that cells use a basic principle of statistical physics, the thermodynamics of phase transitions, to form membraneless compartments. The nominees went on to quantify droplet viscosity, surface tension, coarsening and nucleation in vivo, and Jülicher developed the theory of chemically active droplets, where non-equilibrium reactions suppress Ostwald ripening and set droplet size and division. The work founded a new field connecting soft-matter physics, polymer theory and biology, and it gives a physical framework for understanding protein aggregation diseases such as ALS. Their minimal physical models have been confirmed quantitatively by experiment. This is a clear case of physics giving biology a new way of thinking.
